steps.label: Write A′ and B′ and check the first law
steps.margin_note: First mark. A′ and B′ are written once at the top because both parts use them. Note that 1, 8 and 9 belong to neither A nor B, so they appear in both complements.

recall.must_convey: That A′ and B′ are written first, and that both sides of part (i) come out as {1, 8, 9}.

steps.why: The mark is for the two sides of (i) being computed separately and coming out the same. Computing A′ and B′ once at the top means part (ii) costs almost nothing.
steps.memory_tip: A′ is whatever is left in U once A is taken out — so it always includes the elements in neither set.
common_mistakes: Leaving 1, 8 and 9 out of A′ and B′ because they are in neither A nor B.
Taking the complement of A inside B rather than inside U.
Writing A′ ∩ B′ down as {1, 8, 9} by assuming the law instead of working it out.

steps.label: Check the second law
steps.margin_note: Second mark. A and B share no element, so A ∩ B is the empty set and its complement is the whole of U. Both sides must still be written out.
lines: (ii) A and B have no common element, so  A ∩ B = ∅

recall.must_convey: That A ∩ B = ∅, so (A ∩ B)′ = U, and that A′ ∪ B′ also comes out as U.
accept: A and B have nothing in common so the intersection is empty and its complement is U

steps.why: Both sides have to be written and seen to agree — the question says show, so quoting De Morgan's law by name earns nothing on its own.
steps.memory_tip: De Morgan swaps the symbol: the complement of a union is an intersection, and the complement of an intersection is a union.
common_mistakes: Writing (A ∩ B)′ = ∅, which is the complement rule used backwards.
Writing A ∩ B = ∅ and stopping, without working out A′ ∪ B′.
Missing 8 and 9 from A′ ∪ B′, so the two sides look different.
